factual_methodological.summary: GOV.UK confirms Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026; ONS confirms revised Q2 GDP growth of 0.5% q/q and the cited productivity context; the Bank of England confirms Bank Rate at 3.75% and August CPI at 3.1%.

editorial_publication_readiness.summary: Revision 1 removes the PT-BR localization blockers recorded in revision 0 while preserving figures, argument structure, causal qualifications and scenarios.

novelty_against_existing_country_layer.summary: No canonical United Kingdom country-context dossier exists; the report connects post-Brexit trade, global services, fiscal/monetary autonomy, devolution, energy, industrial policy, defence and regional capital allocation.

visual_evidence_readiness.summary: Both locales contain two tables, four charts and a structural flow; PT-BR chart units and reader-facing terminology are localized in revision 1.

political_neutrality.summary: Officeholders, governments and policy choices are described analytically without partisan or electoral endorsement.

contrary_evidence: The UK retains globally important finance, professional services, science, universities, aerospace, defence, life sciences and clean-energy capabilities.
Stronger 2026 GDP data argue against treating the post-Brexit model as a simple decline story.
Fiscal constraint is material, but monetary sovereignty and deep capital markets change the transmission relative to euro-area sovereigns.
limitations: ONS labour and productivity measures retain published LFS quality caveats.
The March 2026 OBR forecast predates the July change of prime minister and is used as an inherited baseline.
Great Britain clean-power metrics are not identical to whole-UK energy statistics.
Revision 1 changes localization only, not the factual or analytical thesis.
notes: Revision 1 approved after correcting all blocking PT-BR localization defects identified in revision 0 and rechecking primary current data, bilingual parity, taxonomy and visuals.

en.title: United Kingdom: services power, fiscal constraint and the reconstruction of a post-Brexit growth model
en.deck: The UK combines global services, finance, science and defence capabilities with weak productivity, high debt-service costs, post-Brexit trade frictions and an investment challenge spanning housing, energy and regional infrastructure.
en.regime: Post-Brexit capital and productivity reconstruction: global services and institutional flexibility coexist with weak productivity, expensive public debt, regional imbalances and a renewed industrial-energy-security investment cycle.
en.key_risk: Weak productivity and high debt-service costs compress fiscal space before housing, grids, defence and industrial investment raise productive capacity.

publication.selection_rationale: The United Kingdom is explicitly implicated in the existing Europe–Russia–Ukraine conflict-system research but lacked a reusable country-level context. A country dossier is warranted to connect the UK's post-Brexit trade regime, services-export model, productivity problem, fiscal and monetary autonomy, devolution, energy transition, defence-industrial expansion and regional capital allocation.
contrary_evidence: The UK retains globally important finance, professional services, science, universities, aerospace, defence, life sciences and clean-energy capabilities, arguing against a simple post-Brexit decline thesis.
Strong first-half 2026 GDP growth does not by itself resolve the deeper productivity, investment, housing and fiscal constraints; cyclical recovery and structural performance are kept separate.
limitations: ONS labour-market and productivity data are subject to Labour Force Survey quality caveats and revisions.
The latest population estimate is mid-2025 and the latest long-term migration flow is the year ending December 2025.
The March 2026 OBR fiscal forecast predates the July 2026 change of prime minister and is used as an inherited baseline rather than a full current-policy forecast.
Great Britain clean-power metrics exclude Northern Ireland and are not identical to whole-UK energy statistics.
Government industrial, energy and defence targets are policy commitments, not evidence of completed investment or capacity.
Revision 1 localizes reader-facing PT-BR chart units and hybrid terminology rejected in revision 0 without changing figures, causal qualifications, scenarios or conclusions.
